rangoli.title: Rangoli
facts: Rangoli is drawn at the doorstep to welcome guests, and goddess Lakshmi at Diwali.
Every region has its own name for it: kolam in Tamil Nadu, muggu in Andhra and Telangana, alpana in Bengal, mandana in Rajasthan, rangavalli in Karnataka.
Traditional rangoli uses rice flour, coloured powder and flower petals, all things you can sweep away and draw again tomorrow.

kolam.title: Kolam
facts: In Tamil Nadu, kolam is drawn every morning at the threshold, often before sunrise.
The dots are called pulli. A sikku kolam loops one line around them without ever lifting the hand.
Kolam is drawn with rice flour, which also feeds ants and birds: a small daily act of sharing.

block.title: Block printing
facts: Sanganer and Bagru, near Jaipur, have printed cloth by hand with carved wooden blocks for centuries.
Each colour needs its own block, pressed by hand, so no two prints are exactly alike.
Bagru printers use dabu, a mud-resist paste, to keep parts of the cloth from taking the dye.

plate.title: Truck art
facts: "HORN OK PLEASE" is painted on the backs of trucks across India. Where the OK came from is still debated.
Truck painters add eyes, nazar battu and sayings like "Buri nazar wale tera muh kala" to keep the evil eye away.
Truck art is hand-painted with brushes, often in a single sitting, in roadside workshops.

poster.title: Hand-painted signs
facts: Before vinyl printing, every shop board and cinema poster in India was painted by hand.
Sign painters drop-shadow their letters in a second colour so they read from across the street.
Many painters were self-taught apprentices who learned lettering by copying their ustad's boards.

mehendi.title: Mehendi
facts: Mehendi paste is made from the dried, powdered leaves of the henna plant.
It goes on for weddings and festivals like Karva Chauth, Teej and Eid.
The stain starts orange and darkens over a day or two. Everyone has a theory for making it darker.

naam.title: Kolam and you
facts: Kolam patterns are often passed down from mother to daughter, each family with its own favourites.
Big kolams during the month of Margazhi can cover the whole street in front of a house.
A kolam with one unbroken line is said to stand for the endless cycle of life.

diya.title: Diya
facts: Deepavali means "row of lamps": deepa (lamp) and avali (row).
A diya is a small clay lamp with a cotton wick and oil or ghee.
Diyas line doorsteps, windows and balconies so that no corner of the home stays dark.

greeting.title: Festival greetings
facts: Festivals in India are celebrated by visiting family, sharing sweets and drawing at the doorstep.
Elders give blessings, and younger people touch their feet in respect.
On Bhai Dooj, siblings exchange blessings and gifts.

pookalam.title: Pookalam
facts: Pookalam is the flower carpet laid at the doorstep for Onam, Kerala's harvest festival.
It grows over the ten days of Onam: a small ring of flowers on Atham, the first day, and a bigger carpet each day until Thiruvonam.
Thumba, a tiny white flower, is a must in many homes. It is said to be King Mahabali's favourite.
Only loose petals are used, never dyed powder, so a pookalam fades and wilts and is laid fresh again.

bandhani.title: Bandhani
facts: Bandhani comes from bandhan, to tie. The cloth is pinched up and tied with thread, often thousands of tiny knots, before it is dyed.
It is made in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Jamnagar and the towns of Kutch are famous for it.
Dyeing goes from light to dark: yellow first, then red or green, then maroon or black. Each round of knots keeps the colour before it.
Patterns are named for their knots: ekdali is a single dot, trikunti three, chaubundi four.
A bandhani odhni or chaniya choli is a Navratri favourite for garba nights.

phuljhadi.title: Phuljhadi
facts: Phuljhadi means a shower of flowers: phool is a flower, and a jhadi is a shower.
Diwali falls on amavasya, the new-moon night, so the lamps have the dark sky to themselves.
A sparkler's branching sparks are tiny bits of burning iron. A little carbon in the iron makes them burst into stars.
Strontium burns red, barium green and copper blue-green. Blue is the hardest firework colour to make.
Most of India's fireworks are made in and around Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu.
Real sparklers burn at over 1,000°C. Hold one at arm's length and drop the hot wire into a bucket of water.

kathputli.title: Kathputli
facts: Kathputli means a doll (putli) made of wood (kath).
Most kathputlis have no legs. A long skirt sweeps the floor, so they can glide and spin.
The puppeteer speaks through a reed whistle called the boli, and someone out front repeats each line in plain words.
The best-loved kathputli play tells the story of Amar Singh Rathore of Nagaur.
India has string, rod, glove and shadow puppets. Andhra's leather puppets are painted on both sides and throw coloured shadows.
World Puppetry Day is 21 March.

warli.title: Warli
facts: Warli painters use only white: rice paste and water with a little gum, on a red-brown wall.
The brush is a bamboo stick, chewed at the end until it is soft.
Everything starts from three shapes: the circle (sun and moon), the triangle (mountains and trees) and the square.
In the tarpa dance, dancers link arms and wind round the tarpa player in a spiral.
Jivya Soma Mashe of Dahanu took Warli painting from walls to the world. He received the Padma Shri in 2011.
Warli painting has had a Geographical Indication tag since 2014.

patang.title: Patang
facts: Uttarayan means the sun's journey north. Gujarat flies kites on Makar Sankranti, around 14 January.
Kai po che means roughly “I have cut it!”: the shout when your kite cuts another.
A patang is paper on two strips of bamboo: a straight spine and a bow bent across the top.
The kanna, a little bridle of thread, decides how a kite flies.
Glass-coated manja hurts birds. In 2017 the National Green Tribunal banned it, along with nylon string.
On Uttarayan night, paper lanterns called tukkal rise on kite strings.
